title: Extract the email addresses of all employees and return as a comma-separated string using `Collectors.joining(", ")`.

s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** This pairs a `map` projection with the `Collectors.joining(delimiter)` terminal collector, which concatenates a stream of strings into one string separated by the given delimiter. The overload `joining(", ")` places a comma and a space between every pair of elements.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** The office manager at the National Bank of India wants to send one email to all staff, so she needs every address strung together, separated by commas, to paste into the "To" box. She copies each address and writes a comma and space between them. `joining(", ")` is exactly that stringing-together.

**One line to remember:** `Collectors.joining(", ")` glues a stream of strings into one comma-separated string.

sections.s2_technical:
First you project each employee to its email with `map(Employee::getEmail)`, producing a stream of email strings. Then the terminal collector `Collectors.joining(", ")` concatenates them into a single string, inserting the delimiter — a comma followed by a space — between consecutive elements but not at the very start or very end.

`joining` has three overloads. With no argument it simply concatenates with nothing between. With one argument it uses that string as the delimiter, which is what we want here. With three arguments `joining(delimiter, prefix, suffix)` it also wraps the whole result, for example `joining(", ", "[", "]")` produces a bracketed list — handy for building a readable summary.

Under the hood joining uses a `StringJoiner`, which is efficient because it appends to a single growing buffer rather than creating a new string for each concatenation. That matters for large lists, where naive string addition in a loop would create many throwaway intermediate strings and perform poorly.

A senior nuance: joining only works on a stream of `CharSequence`, so you must map to strings first. If some emails might be null, filter them out before joining, because a null would throw a null pointer exception during concatenation. Guarding the data before the join keeps the output clean and crash-free.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India's office manager needs to send a single circular email to all staff and wants every employee's address in one comma-separated line to paste into the recipient field. The HR system holds employees as objects, so we must pull out each email and stitch them together with a comma and space. This is exactly how map plus joining works — each employee is projected to its email and the stream of emails is concatenated into one delimited string.

The code defines an `Employee` with name and email. A `MailingListService` exposes `recipientLine(List<Employee>)` using map then joining with a null filter. The runnable `Main` feeds employees including one with a null email and logs the final recipient string.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: Rajesh, Priya, Amit (null email), Neha.

Step 1: The stream opens over four employees.

Step 2: map projects each to its email, producing the stream rajesh address, priya address, null, neha address.

Step 3: The filter drops the null email belonging to Amit, so the stream now carries only three real addresses. This protects the join from a null pointer exception.

Step 4: joining with the comma-space delimiter starts with the first address, then appends a comma and space followed by the next address, and so on, building one growing string in a StringJoiner buffer.

Step 5: The delimiter is placed only between elements, so there is no trailing comma after the last address.

Step 6: The terminal returns the single concatenated recipient string.

```
Oct 30, 2026 11:45:02 AM com.bank.mail.service.MailingListService recipientLine
INFO: Building recipient line from 4 employees
Oct 30, 2026 11:45:02 AM com.bank.mail.Main lambda$main$0
INFO: To: rajesh@nationalbank.co.in, priya@nationalbank.co.in, neha@nationalbank.co.in
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  Input: [Rajesh, Priya, Amit(null email), Neha]
    │
    ▼
  map(getEmail)  → [rajesh@..., priya@..., null, neha@...]
    │
    ▼
  filter(email != null)  → [rajesh@..., priya@..., neha@...]  (Amit dropped)
    │
    ▼
  collect(joining(", "))   (StringJoiner buffer, delimiter BETWEEN only)
    rajesh@... + ", " + priya@... + ", " + neha@...
    │
    ▼
  Result: "rajesh@..., priya@..., neha@..."  (no trailing comma)
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
To turn a stream of strings into one delimited string I use the joining collector, giving it the delimiter I want between elements. Here I first mapped each employee to its email to get a stream of strings, then collected with joining of a comma and a space, which concatenates all the addresses into one line with a comma and space between each, and importantly no delimiter before the first or after the last.

In my banking project at the National Bank of India this built the recipient line for a staff circular, where the office manager needed every address in one comma-separated string to paste into the To field. I projected each employee to its email and joined them into a single string.

A senior point I add is awareness of the joining overloads and the null trap. Joining comes in three forms: no argument for plain concatenation, one argument for a delimiter, and a three-argument form that also wraps the whole thing with a prefix and suffix, which is handy for a bracketed summary. Under the hood it uses a StringJoiner, so it appends to one growing buffer rather than creating a throwaway string per concatenation, which performs well on large lists. Crucially, joining only accepts strings, and a null in the stream would throw a null pointer exception during concatenation, so I filter out null emails before the join to keep the output clean and the code crash-free.
